title: How to create a virtual machine using qemu+kvm
text:
To create virtual machines using qemu+kvm under Rocky Linux, we need to install the necessary packages and set up the environment.
First, we need to install the required packages and start the libvirt service:
sudo dnf install -y virt-install libvirt qemu-kvm libguestfs-tools
sudo systemctl enable --now libvirtd
If a personal computer is used, probably not much space is allocated for the /var directory, which is the default location for storing virtual machine images. To avoid running out of space, we can create a directory under /home to store the images and give libvirt/qemu permission to access it:
cd /home
sudo mkdir vms
sudo chown $USER:$USER vms
sudo chmod 711 vms
# tell selinux to allow libvirt to access the directory and files therein
sudo semanage fcontext -a -t virt_image_t "/home/vms(/.*)?"
# apply the new context to the existing files and directories
sudo restorecon -R -v /home/vms
Through my test, 711 is minimum permission for the directory /home/vms to allow libvirt to access it. If it is 700, libvirt will complain about permission denied when trying to access the image file in that directory.
For convenience, we can make our own user a member of the libvirt group [1], so that we can manage virtual machines without sudo:
sudo usermod -a -G libvirt $USER
To ensure that the new group membership is effective, we can log out and log back in.
We also need to set the LIBVIRT_DEFAULT_URI environment variable to point to the system-wide libvirt instance qemu:///system. Otherwise, the default is qemu:///session pointing to the user session.
export LIBVIRT_DEFAULT_URI="qemu:///system"
We can add the above line to our shell profile (e.g., ~/.bashrc or ~/.zshrc) to make it permanent.

title: How to create a virtual machine using qemu+kvm
text:
Network setup
Next, we need to prepare the network for the virtual machines. By default, libvirt provides a NATed network called “default”. We can start it and set it to autostart:
virsh net-start default
virsh net-autostart default
If somehow the default network is not available, we can create it using the default XML configuration file provided by libvirt:
virsh net-define /usr/share/libvirt/networks/default.xml
At this moment it is sufficient to use the default network for our virtual machines. For more advanced network configuration, please refer to the official documentation [2-3].

title: How to create a virtual machine using qemu+kvm
text:
Image preparation
To prepare the image for the virtual machine, we could take advantage of the cloud image provided by Rocky Linux, which is a qcow2 image with cloud-init pre-installed.
We can then utilise the virt-customize tool to customize the image, such as setting the password for the root user, creating a test user, and resizing the image to have enough space for the root partition. Below is an example of how to do this:
# let virt-customize access the image file directly without using libvirt, which is faster and more efficient
VM_NAME=$1
export LIBGUESTFS_BACKEND=direct
IMAGE_DIR="/home/vms"
# assumming the cloud image is already downloaded to $IMAGE_DIR, and its name is Rocky-9-GenericCloud-Base.latest.x86_64.qcow2
IMAGE="$IMAGE_DIR/Rocky-9-GenericCloud-Base.latest.x86_64.qcow2"
cp "$IMAGE" "$IMAGE_DIR/$VM_NAME.qcow2"
# Resize the image to 40G to have enough space for the root partition
qemu-img resize "$IMAGE_DIR/$VM_NAME.qcow2" 40G
# Customize the image
# Replace TESTUSER and TESTUSERPASSWORD with your own username and password for the test user
# The root user will be locked and cannot be used to log in
virt-customize -a "$IMAGE_DIR/$VM_NAME.qcow2" \
    --run-command "passwd -l root" \
    --run-command "usermod -L root" \
    --edit '/etc/passwd: s/^root:x:0:0:root:\/root:\/bin\/bash/root:x:0:0:root:\/root:\/sbin\/nologin/' \
    --hostname "$VM_NAME" \
    --password TESTUSER:password:TESTUSERPASSWORD \
    --run-command "useradd -m -G wheel TESTUSER" \
    --edit '/etc/default/grub: s/GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX=\"/GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX=\"console=tty0 console=ttyS0,115200n8 /' \
    --run-command "grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/grub2/grub.cfg" \
    --run-command 'growpart /dev/sda 4 || growpart /dev/sda 3' \
    --run-command 'xfs_growfs /' \
    --uninstall cloud-init \
In the virt-customize command, the arguments
--edit '/etc/default/grub: s/GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX=\"/GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX=\"console=tty0 console=ttyS0,115200n8 /' \
--run-command "grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/grub2/grub.cfg" \
are used to enable the serial console, which is necessary for us to access the virtual machine through the serial console later.
The argument
--run-command 'growpart /dev/sda 4 || growpart /dev/sda 3'
tries to grow the partition 4 of the disk /dev/sda, which is the root partition in the cloud image. If it fails (e.g., because there are only 3 partitions), it will try to grow partition 3 instead.

title: How to create a virtual machine using qemu+kvm
text:
Virtual machine creation
To create the virtual machine, we can use the virt-install command. Below is an example of how to do this:
export LIBGUESTFS_BACKEND=direct
VM_NAME=$1
IMAGE_NAME=$2
IMAGE_DIR="/home/vms"
virt-install \
--name "$VM_NAME" \
--ram 4096 \
--vcpus 2 \
--cpu host-passthrough \
--os-variant rocky9 \
--disk path="$IMAGE_DIR/$VM_NAME.qcow2",bus=virtio \
--network network=default \
--import \
--graphics none \
--boot uefi \
--serial pty \
--console pty,target_type=serial \
--noautoconsole
In this example, 4GB of RAM and 2 vCPUs are allocated to the virtual machine.
After creation, if you would like to remove the virtual machine, you can use the virsh undefine command:
virsh undefine "$VM_NAME" --remove-all-storage --nvram
To do this, you need to make sure that the virtual machine is shut down first

title: How to create a virtual machine using qemu+kvm
text:
Daily operation
To show the console of the virtual machine, we can use the virsh console command:
virsh console "$VM_NAME"
To shut down the virtual machine, we can use the virsh shutdown command:
virsh shutdown "$VM_NAME"

References
[1] Setting Up libvirt on Rocky Linux - RockyLinux
[2] Network XML format - libvirt
[3] Managing Virtual Networks- RedHat

title: How to deploy 2FA for ssh access using Google Authenticator on Rocky Linux
text: In this post, we introduce how to deploy 2FA for ssh access using Google Authenticator on Rocky Linux 9.7. The process is mainly divided into the following steps:

title: How to deploy 2FA for ssh access using Google Authenticator on Rocky Linux
text:
Install Google Authenticator
The google-authenticator package is available in the EPEL repository.
To enable the EPEL repository, we can use the following command:
sudo dnf install epel-release
After this, we can install the google-authenticator package using the following command:
sudo dnf install google-authenticator

title: How to deploy 2FA for ssh access using Google Authenticator on Rocky Linux
text:
Configure sshd
Edit the /etc/ssh/sshd_config file, and change/add the following lines:
# /etc/ssh/sshd_config
KbdInteractiveAuthentication yes
UsePAM yes
ChallengeResponseAuthentication yes
AuthenticationMethods password keyboard-interactive
Depend on the method, password might be changed to the publickey etc.

title: How to deploy 2FA for ssh access using Google Authenticator on Rocky Linux
text:
Configure pam.d
Edit the /etc/pam.d/sshd file, and add the following line at the end of the file:
auth       required     pam_google_authenticator.so secret=${HOME}/.ssh/.google_authenticator echo_verification_code [authtok_prompt=Your secret token: ]
We can modify authtok_prompt to customize the prompt message. For example, we can change it to authtok_prompt=Your 2FA token:.
To satisfy SELinux, .google_authenticator file is into the ~/.ssh/ directory.

title: How to deploy 2FA for ssh access using Google Authenticator on Rocky Linux
text:
Configure Google-Authenticator for your account
Under the account you want to enable 2FA, run the following command:
google-authenticator
and follows the instructions.
Consideration might be needed for the option --disallow-reuse. If it is enabled, some remote access tools may not work properly e.g., thinlinc client which needs to verify the token twice.

title: How to deploy 2FA for ssh access using Google Authenticator on Rocky Linux
text:
Test
Now we can test if the 2FA is working or not by log out and log in again. It is important to note that a mistake in deploying 2FA may result in a lockout of the account. Therefore, it is recommended to always keep a ssh session alive when configuring 2FA and testing.

title: Deploy Nextcloud using podman on Rockylinux 10
text:
Nextcloud is a open source suite for deploying a cloud service like OneDrive and Dropbox at home. It also provides client versions for various platform including Linux. In this post, We will share the experience on deploy Nextcloud using podman on a small home server operating Rockylinux 10.
First, we create a podman-compose.yml file [1,2] for pulling the image and building the service.
version: '3'
services:
  # Redis for caching and file locking [3]
  redis:
    image: redis:alpine
    container_name: nextcloud-redis
    restart: always
    volumes:
      - ./redis:/data
    # Replace <redis-password> with your actual password
    command: redis-server --requirepass <redis-password> --maxmemory 1G --maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru
    networks:
      - nextcloud-net
    security_opt:
      - label=disable
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          cpus: '0.5'
          memory: 1.5G
  # MariaDB database
  db:
    image: mariadb:10.11
    container_name: nextcloud-db
    restart: always
    environment:
      # Replace these with your actual credentials
      - MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=<db-root-password>
      - MYSQL_DATABASE=nextcloud
      - MYSQL_USER=nextcloud
      - MYSQL_PASSWORD=<db-user-password>
      - MYSQL_INITDB_SKIP_TZINFO=1
    volumes:
      - ./db:/var/lib/mysql
      - ./my.cnf:/etc/mysql/conf.d/my.cnf
    networks:
      - nextcloud-net
    security_opt:
      - label=disable
    tmpfs:
      - /tmp:size=2G
      # Optional: enable if you want Nextcloud to wait for DB readiness before automatic DB setup
      # healthcheck:
      #   test: ["CMD", "mysqladmin", "ping", "-h", "localhost", "-p<db-root-password>"]
      #   interval: 5s
      #   timeout: 3s
      #   retries: 10
      #   start_period: 10s
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          cpus: '1'
          memory: 2G
  # Nextcloud application
  app:
    image: nextcloud:stable
    container_name: nextcloud-app
    restart: always
    # Optional: enable if using healthchecks
    # depends_on:
    #   db:
    #     condition: service_healthy
    #   redis:
    #     condition: service_started
    depends_on:
      - db
      - redis
    environment:
      # Replace with your actual domain/host
      - NEXTCLOUD_TRUSTED_DOMAINS=<your-domain>
      - NEXTCLOUD_OVERWRITEPROTOCOL=http
      - NEXTCLOUD_OVERWRITEHOST=<your-host>
      - NEXTCLOUD_OVERWRITEWEBROOT=/
      # Optional: enable automatic Redis integration
      # - REDIS_HOST=redis
      # - REDIS_HOST_PASSWORD=<redis-password
      # Optional: enable automatic DB setup
      # - MYSQL_HOST=db
      # - MYSQL_DATABASE=nextcloud
      # - MYSQL_USER=nextcloud
      # - MYSQL_PASSWORD=<db-user-password>
    volumes:
      - ./nextcloud-data:/var/www/html
    networks:
      - nextcloud-net
    ports:
      - "10000:80"
    security_opt:
      - label=disable
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          cpus: '2'
          memory: 8G
networks:
  nextcloud-net:
    driver: bridge
To start and stop the service using podman, using
podman-compose up -d
podman-compose down
During the first podman-compose up call, containers will be built by pulling the image from the chosen repositories.
To check redis is enabled for Nextcloud, find the file config.php at the directory /var/www/html inside the container or ./nextcloud-data at host, and check for the following configuration:
'memcache.local' => '\\OC\\Memcache\\APCu',
'memcache.distributed' => '\\OC\\Memcache\\Redis',
'memcache.locking' => '\\OC\\Memcache\\Redis',
In this way, a deployment of Nextcloud is finished. We may configure further, say, to enable reverse proxy for the website. It is worthwhile to the optional settings are to be tested.
[1] https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/devops/compose-files-with-podman/
[2] https://docs.docker.com/reference/compose-file/
[3] https://docs.nextcloud.com/server/19/admin_manual/configuration_server/caching_configuration.html

title: Timestamp in Bash history
text:
On Linux systems—especially in cluster environments—it’s often necessary to review the history of commands that have been executed. By default, however, Bash does not display timestamps for commands in history.
To enable timestamps, set the HISTTIMEFORMAT environment variable in the .bashrc file.
Below is an example section of a .bashrc file that configures Bash to record and display timestamps in command history. Line 2 allows each node or server to have its own history file, which is particularly useful in cluster environments where multiple nodes share the same storage. Lines 11-14 ensure that the records are synchronized if multiple sessions, e.g., tmux or screen, are running at the same time.
#Set the history file according to hostname
export HISTFILE="$HOME/.bash_history_$(hostname -s)"
#Show the timestamp as day-month-year time
export HISTTIMEFORMAT="%d/%m/%y %T "
#Set the number of commands recorded in the memory
export HISTSIZE=1000
#Set the number of command recorded in the file specified by HISTFILE
export HISTFILESIZE=10000
#Store multi-line commands in one history entry
shopt -s cmdhist
#Append commands to the history
shopt -s histappend
#Save each command right after it has been executed.
export PROMPT_COMMAND="history -a;history -n"

title: Concise Modern C++: A Bridge from Python, MATLAB, and Mathematica
text:
C++ is a powerful programming language that supports a wide range of scientific computing applications and provides the computational backbone for the AI revolution. Modern features have been gradually added to C++, simplifying the development of scientific applications. However, these features often involve complex concepts and techniques—particularly template programming—which results in a steep learning curve.
This article connects and compares key features of modern C++ with other languages used in scientific computing, including Mathematica, Python, and MATLAB. We will find that many modern C++ features are fundamentally the same as those in other research-oriented languages, differing only in their syntax and implementation details.

Summary
In this article, we have introduced some key features of modern C++ for scientific computing, including containers, algorithms, and lambda expressions. We have also compared these features with their counterparts in other languages commonly used in scientific computing, such as Mathematica, Python, and MATLAB.
While the syntax and specific implementations may differ, we can migrate our concept learned from other languages, like Python, MATLAB, and Mathematica, and use modern C++ to write concise but performant code for scientific computing applications.

title: Subtle router configuration breaking the VPN and Teams calls
text:
Recently, a subtle router configuration broke the VPN and Teams calls. The symptoms were intermittent VPN disconnections and Teams calls freezing periodically before recovering. Various measurements, such as tuning the MTU value, were tried but proved ineffective. The tricky part was that everything else appeared to work fine except for these two tasks.
By chance, I discovered that when sitting very close to the router, both the VPN and Teams calls worked fine. When I moved farther away, both began to fail again. However, further testing revealed that distance was not the critical factor. The primary issue was a router configuration called band steering, which combined the 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz bands under a single SSID and automatically switched devices between them. After disabling band steering and separating the bands, the connection became stable. At a distance farther from the router, the signal experiences slightly more severe fluctuation, which may cause the router to quietly switch between 5G and 2.4G. This kind of switching is problematic for VPN and Teams calls, which require stable, real-time communication. After disabling band steering and allowing the device to manually select either 2.4G or 5G, both the VPN and Teams calls now work reliably, even at distance.

title: Rocky Linux 10 first installation
text:
Rocky Linux 10 was released on 11-Jun-2025, which ships with GCC 14.2.1, Python 3.12.9, and the Linux kernel 6.12.0 etc, see the Rocky Linux Release and Version Guide, the news article and the release notes.
It is found that xrdp appears missing from even the EPEL repository (e.g., see this thread in the Rocky Linux Forum). This is likely related to the replacements of XOrg Server with Wayland and VNC with the Remote Desktop Protocol for default graphical remote access.
To enable the graphical remote access, we can use the GNOME’s built-in remote desktop feature, please see Mahdi’s article for setup.
Often we would like to change the port number for enhancing security, please see this discourse thread for the steps.
For further information about the replacement of Xorg server, please see Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10 plans for Wayland and Xorg server.

title: Concepts of virtualisation
text:
There are several layers of virtualisation. Bare Metal is the hardware. A Hypervisor is the software that manages that hardware for VMs. Type 1 (ESXi, KVM, Hyper-V) sits directly on the hardware for maximum speed. Type 2 (VirtualBox) sits on an OS for convenience. QEMU is the “utility player”—it provides the virtual hardware (keyboard/disk) to KVM, or acts as a standalone (but slow) emulator.

Bare Metal: The raw, physical hardware (CPU, RAM, Disk). It’s the “metal” server rack with nothing installed on it yet.
Hypervisor: The manager. It’s the software layer that sits on the hardware to create and run Virtual Machines (VMs). It’s the “boss” that decides how much RAM each VM gets.
There are two types of hypervisors: Type 1 and Type 2.
Type 1 hypervisors boot directly on the physical server to run multiple virtual machines at maximum efficiency.
They include:

VMware ESXi: It is its own tiny operating system. When the computer turns on, ESXi loads first, then starts your VMs. There is no “middleman.”
Microsoft Hyper-V: This is a “stealth” Type 1. When you enable Hyper-V on Windows, it actually slides underneath your Windows OS. Windows itself becomes a “special VM” (management partition), giving Hyper-V direct control of the hardware.

KVM: It converts the Linux Kernel into the hypervisor. Since the Kernel owns the hardware, KVM operates at the lowest possible level.
Type 2 hypervisors run as an application on top of an existing OS. You use your computer normally, open the hypervisor software, and launch a VM inside a window. Such hypervisors typically include Oracle VirtualBox and VMware Workstation. They are easy to set up and use, while their performance is lower than Type 1 ones in principle.
QEMU is a special one: if working with KVM, it is a part of a Type 1 hypervisor setup, but it can also work alone, which acts as an emulator. When working with KVM, it emulates “extra” hardware the VM needs (like a mouse, keyboard, or disk drive) that isn’t handled by the KVM engine.
Guest virtual machine: An independent software instance of an operating system that runs on top of a hypervisor.
Container Engine (Docker/containerd/Apptainer/podman): Runs on the Guest VM (or bare metal) to host containers.
Think of a VM like a standalone house—it has its own plumbing, heating, and infrastructure. A container is like an apartment in a building—it has its own front door and space, but it shares the building’s main infrastructure (the OS).
Virtual Machines: Each VM includes a full copy of an operating system (OS), the application, and necessary drivers. They run on a “hypervisor” that mimics hardware, making them heavy and slow to start, but very secure and isolated.
Containers: Containers share the host’s OS kernel and only package the application and its dependencies. This makes them incredibly lightweight, fast to boot, and highly portable across different environments.
Containers can be created and run inside a VM.

title: Concepts of virtualisation
text:
Management
There are also tools for managing virtual machines and containers. Locally, there are libvirt (KVM) and VBoxManage (VirtualBox) for dealing with virtual machines, and Docker CLI, Apptainer CLI, and Podman CLI for dealing with containers. Apart from them, there are also higher-level management tools like OpenStack for managing many virtual machines and K8s for containers.
